title: Ruth and Jonah
intro: 20 days through two short Bible stories, Ruth and Jonah, one verse at a time.

posts.caption: Starting today, 20 days through two of the Bible's shortest stories: Ruth, then Jonah. Ruth is set in the time of the judges, before Israel had kings. A famine drives one family out of Bethlehem, whose name means "house of bread," to Moab, a neighboring nation east of the Dead Sea.

Naomi's husband and both sons have died in Moab, and she is going home to Bethlehem. She urges her two widowed Moabite daughters-in-law to go back to their own families. Orpah does, but Ruth refuses with these words. They are now often read at weddings, though Ruth spoke them to her mother-in-law.

Naomi arrives back in Bethlehem, and the town's women can hardly believe it's her. In Hebrew, Naomi means "pleasant" and Mara means "bitter." "The Almighty" translates Shaddai, an ancient name for God. She left with a husband and two sons and has come back with only Ruth.

Israel's law told farmers to leave the edges of their fields and any dropped grain for the poor, widows, and foreigners to gather, a practice called gleaning (Leviticus 19 and Deuteronomy 24). Ruth is all three. The narrator says she just "happened" to pick Boaz's field, and many readers hear a wink in that word.

Boaz, the landowner, has heard how Ruth left her own parents and homeland to stay with Naomi, and he blesses her. The Hebrew word for "wings" here, kanaf, also means the corner or edge of a garment. The same word returns at a key moment in the next chapter.

Ruth comes home with a big load of barley, and Naomi learns whose field it was. The "kindness" she praises is hesed, a key word in Ruth: loyal love that goes beyond what duty requires. A kinsman-redeemer, or go'el, was a close relative responsible for rescuing family in trouble, such as buying back land they had lost.

On Naomi's advice, Ruth goes at night to the threshing floor where Boaz is sleeping after the harvest, and lies down at his feet. "Corner of your garment" is kanaf, the same word as the "wings" in Boaz's blessing. Spreading a garment over someone was a way of describing marriage (compare Ezekiel 16:8), so in effect Ruth asks Boaz to become the answer to his own blessing.

Boaz agrees, though a closer relative has the first right to redeem. "A woman of noble character" is eshet chayil in Hebrew, the same phrase that opens the famous poem at the end of Proverbs (31:10), and in some Hebrew Bibles the book of Ruth comes right after Proverbs. The narrator used a matching phrase for Boaz in chapter 2.

Boaz settles the matter at the town gate, marries Ruth, and they have a son. The women of Bethlehem, who heard Naomi call herself empty, now celebrate with her. Seven was a number of completeness, and sons meant security in old age, so this is very high praise for a foreign daughter-in-law.

The twist at the end: Ruth, the outsider from Moab, becomes the great-grandmother of King David. Matthew's Gospel later names her in the family line of Jesus (Matthew 1:5). Jews traditionally read the book of Ruth at Shavuot, the early-summer festival of the wheat harvest. That's Ruth; Jonah comes next.

From Ruth we turn to Jonah, a very different short story. Jonah, whose name means "dove," is a prophet also mentioned in 2 Kings 14:25. God sends him to Nineveh, a great city of Assyria, Israel's feared enemy, whose ruins lie in Mosul, Iraq. Instead he sails from Joppa for Tarshish, a distant port in the opposite direction, possibly in Spain.

God sends a violent storm, and the terrified sailors cast lots to find out who is to blame. The lot falls on Jonah, and this is his answer. The irony is hard to miss: he worships the God who made the sea, and he is trying to escape that God by sea.

The storm keeps getting worse, and Jonah tells the sailors to throw him overboard. Instead they row hard for land, and they pray to Jonah's God before they finally do it. Many readers notice that these foreign sailors come across as more decent, and more open to God, than the prophet himself.

The Hebrew says "a great fish," not a whale. The whale came later, partly through English translations like the King James Version, which says "whale" in Matthew 12:40, where Jesus compares his own three days in the grave to Jonah's. In Hebrew Bibles, this verse is numbered as the first verse of chapter 2.

Jonah's prayer from inside the fish is written as a psalm, and several lines echo the book of Psalms (compare Psalm 120:1). Sheol is the Hebrew name for the realm of the dead, so Jonah describes himself as already as good as dead. At the end of the prayer, the fish spits him out onto dry land.

God tells Jonah a second time to go, and this time he does. In Hebrew his whole message is just five words. The verb for "overturned" is the one used for the destruction of Sodom, but it can also mean "turned around" or "changed," a double meaning many readers notice once they see how the story ends.

Nineveh listens. The king trades his robe for sackcloth and orders a fast for people and even animals, saying, "Who knows? God may turn and relent." God does. Jonah is read in synagogues on the afternoon of Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, whose theme is repentance.

posts.display: “This is why I was so quick to flee toward Tarshish. I knew that You are a gracious and compassionate God, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion—One who relents from sending disaster.”
posts.caption: Instead of celebrating, Jonah is furious, and now he explains why he ran in the first place. He echoes God's description of himself to Moses in Exodus 34:6, one of the most repeated lines in the Hebrew Bible. By his own account, Jonah fled because he expected God to forgive Nineveh.

Jonah sits outside the city to see what will happen. God "appoints" a plant for shade, then a worm to kill it, then a scorching wind, the same verb used for the great fish. When Jerome's Latin translation called this plant "ivy" instead of the familiar "gourd," Augustine wrote that it caused an uproar in one North African congregation.

Jonah is angry that his shade plant died, and God answers with this question. The book ends right there, without Jonah's reply. People who "cannot tell their right hand from their left" may mean small children, or people without moral guidance. That's Ruth and Jonah. Thank you for reading them with me.
